description: KMD Labs is a three-person geoinformatics team — Adrian Kulik, Leszek Michalak and Marcin Derewońko — formed after reaching the CASSINI Hackathon final. We work at the intersection of satellite remote sensing, ML-based anomaly detection and software engineering, turning Earth observation archives into interactive tools scientists and responders can act on.
summary:
For NASA Space Apps Challenge 15, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots, we built an interactive wildfire activity calendar. It shows a 2D map and a 3D globe, backed by a Python API that pulls NASA FIRMS data on demand for any area and date range the user selects.

The challenge is that MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) are not directly comparable. VIIRS detects about four times more hotspots, so simply adding up detections makes it look as if fire activity jumped when the new satellites arrived.

Our model treats all five satellites as independent witnesses of the same fires. It divides all detections by each satellite's measured efficiency and operating time, and expresses the result in MODIS-equivalent hotspots. The latest version also corrects for MODIS orbit drift and keeps the series going after Suomi NPP stopped in November 2026. Every result comes with a calibrated 90% interval and was tested against MODIS on years the model had not seen.

This matters because MODIS is nearing the end of its mission. Without harmonization, the 26-year fire record would break, and with it any reliable comparison of current fire seasons against history.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
A user picks an area on a 2D map or 3D globe and sets a date range. The FastAPI backend downloads only the matching NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS detections and caches them. It then:

  • Bins detections into H3 hexagons and months, separately for day and night.
  • Measures each satellite’s efficiency (hotspots reported per MODIS hotspot) on overlap months, pulled towards regional values so small areas don’t produce noise.
  • Divides all detections by the satellites’ combined sensing power (efficiency × operating time). The result is in MODIS-equivalent hotspots, the maximum-likelihood estimate under a Poisson model.
  • Corrects MODIS orbit drift and chains NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 to Suomi NPP (v4).
  • Reports a 90% interval calibrated on blocked k-fold validation, and marks months never downloaded as missing, not zero.

The panel shows a burning calendar, history charts with the interval, a multi-year anomaly and CSV/JSON/SVG/PNG exports.

What benefits does it have?

  • One comparable series from 2000 to today: the 2012 VIIRS start no longer looks like a jump in fire activity.
  • Honest uncertainty: every monthly value has an interval, and missing data reads as missing.
  • Any area, any period, with no API key needed for viewing.
  • Transparent: the method is explained in a glossary and every hotspot can be exported.

What is the intended impact?
MODIS is nearing the end of its mission. Without harmonization the 26-year record breaks, and so do comparisons of current fire seasons with history. The tool lets researchers, land managers and the public compare a season with past years on one scale, with a clear statement of how certain each value is.

Tools, languages, software and hardware

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, H3, pytest.
  • Frontend: Angular 21, TypeScript, Three.js, Canvas 2D, d3-geo, SCSS, the KMD design system, offline cache.
  • Infrastructure: Docker, Google Cloud Run, GitHub.
  • Hardware: standard laptops.

How is the project creative?

  • Satellites as witnesses: each satellite’s efficiency is estimated per area, month and day/night, so adding or losing one changes the precision, not the level.
  • Orbit drift is modelled from the satellites’ own acquisition times, and the record continues past Suomi NPP’s end in November 2026.
  • Fires only VIIRS can see are kept as a separate explanatory layer.
  • Hotspot clusters pulse on the map in colours that stay distinguishable on colour-blind-safe palettes.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Validation honesty: blocked k-fold by years, forward tests, and weak spots stated openly (the 2024 overestimate, noise in small areas).
  • Data limits: a hotspot is not a fire; clouds, smoke and overpass times hide fires; few detections mean wide intervals.
  • FIRMS rate limits: on-demand download and caching.
  • Licensing: Esri imagery replaced with NASA GIBS, attributions complete.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, reduced motion, screen-reader text, Polish and English.
  • Clear wording: “hotspots” instead of “fires”, no misleading “live” labels.
